title: This site
lead: A portfolio built as a product: a static build, a look of its own for every page, an open log of decisions and checks before every commit.

brief.whatText: A site in two languages: home, Pora na Paru, Flow and Projects. It is plain files with no application server, served by Caddy.
brief.roleText: Design, front end, motion, infrastructure and copy.
brief.openText: The code, the log of decisions and the plan are on GitHub. Each section links to its files.

steps.refuse: Refuses unless on main, with a clean tree, level with GitHub
steps.copy: A copy in a folder of the commit under releases/, equal files as hard links
steps.switch: An atomic switch of the current link
steps.verify: A check of the real domain: codes, CSP, redirects
steps.back: If it fails, the link returns to the last release

form.name: Form
form.title: Every page has a form of its own
form.p1: A portfolio usually describes the work in words. Here a page is built like the work itself: home is a stage that scrolls down and sideways, Pora na Paru is a week of the product's own schedule, Flow looks like Obsidian because that case was a base of notes, and Projects looks like an editor because I am a designer.
form.p2: The price of that form is an engine per page. To keep them from growing together, pages are split by boundaries: a feature does not import another, and what they share moves down to <c>ui/</c> and <c>lib/</c>. It is an ESLint rule rather than an agreement: an import across a boundary fails the check.

themes.name: Themes
themes.title: One component, four themes
themes.p1: Each page declares a theme, and the theme changes colours, typefaces and the look of controls. There are two modes, so eight combinations. A component knows nothing of themes: it reads tokens, and the values live in the theme's file. A new theme is one file.
themes.p2: A colour outside the contract does not compile: the Tailwind palette is off. A test measures contrast, and that is why a theme has two accents. <c>accent</c> is the exact brand colour for fills, <c>accent-strong</c> is the one for text. White on the product's blue gives 3.7:1, too little for text.
themes.p3: The theme is declared in the markup and read through <c>:has()</c>, so it is in the first HTML and the page does not flash. <c>\Get in touch</c> on home and <c>[[Get in touch]]</c> on Flow are one component, and the capsule changes its skin on the fly when a chapter of another theme arrives on home. The values below are read from the sample at every switch.

lens.name: Lens
lens.title: Design and code on one screen
lens.p1: The first screen is two layers: the design and its blueprint, with sizes and real lines of code. A test finds those lines in the sources, so the blueprint cannot drift from the code.
lens.p2: The layers match to the pixel: every block of the blueprint stands where the real one does, because the block itself lies inside it, hidden, and sets its size. The lens only opens the second layer with <c>clip-path</c>. It reaches the capsule too, though that lies outside the first screen: a script writes it the same variables in its own coordinates.
lens.p3: The first screen never waits for animation. The name is in the HTML and drawn from the first frame, and the assembly only wipes an outline off it. The real controls lie under the code layer and take the clicks, and keyboard focus lifts them above it.

motion.name: Motion
motion.title: A page change along the slash of the logo
motion.p1: Each tool has its zone: CSS does hover and focus, <c>ViewTransition</c> the page change, GSAP the scenes on scroll, canvas the graphs and lines. Durations and curves live in tokens, so an effect's code holds no numbers.
motion.p2: The first page change looked bad. A <c>ViewTransition</c> around the page makes one layer as tall as the page, 40,321 px on home on 05.11.2026, and the browser squeezes it to the screen. Now only the screen is captured, and the new page arrives along a 20.2° line, the lean of the slash in the logo. A step back in the capsule runs the other way.
motion.p3: In Firefox the shape stood at its end for the whole change: it does not interpolate a registered <c>@property</c> variable on these pseudo-elements. So the shapes are written out in <c>polygon</c> keyframes. WebDriver's screenshot does not show this, so that frame comes from a system capture of a real browser window.
motion.p4: Then it turned out the change was waiting for home. Leaving, it put every GSAP animation back to its start, even those never played, and arriving, it built its scenes inside the transition's update. In Zen the page stood still for 1.6 s after a click, and the slash flashed at the end. Now a page that leaves drops its animations where they stand, and a page that arrives builds its scenes after the slash: 165 ms from the click to the start of the change, measured 05.11.2026.

week.name: Week
week.title: The product instead of screenshots
week.p1: The Pora na Paru page does not tell about the product, it shows it: it is the product's schedule in a browser. The week's lessons are chapters, a lesson's type says what is inside, and a lesson's window opens as in the product. The values come from its design system, made 1.25 times larger: here the cards are read, not skimmed.
week.p2: The times are a real university's, while today, the line of the time and the lesson going on follow the reader's clock. The page is built long before anyone opens it, so a script sets the dates, and without it the week reads without them. The scrollbar is drawn, as the product's is: the system's went away when the window took the scroll, and the page shifted.
week.p3: There is no blur under the lesson's window, though the product has one: Zen repainted the blurred screen on every frame of a change of lessons, and the window ran at 30 frames instead of 60. The glass stayed on the capsule, a strip of 540 by 41 px, where a measurement gave the same 60 frames.

previews.name: Previews
previews.title: A link's picture from the same tokens
previews.p1: Every page has a link picture of its own in each language, twelve files. A script assembles them from the site's themes, strings and logo, photographs them in Playwright and writes the PNGs and a manifest with a hash of the sources. Flow, Pora na Paru and Projects show the page itself in a window.
previews.p2: A stale picture fails the checks: Unit compares the hash with the manifest. Flow's card draws the real graph, and its simulation ends on different coordinates on arm64 and x64, so the hash counts the graph's notes and links, not its points.

gates.name: Checks
gates.title: 14 checks, one command
gates.p1: <c>python3 scripts/check.py</c> runs before every commit, and CI runs the same command on a PR. Below is a real run of {date}: {unit} unit tests and {browser} browser tests.
gates.p2: The browser checks run behind a real Caddy, the same image digest as the server: addresses, headers, CSP, accessibility in both modes, scenes with reduced motion and without JavaScript. A check must be able to fail: the scaffold was tested with a deliberate import across a boundary and with text in the markup.
gates.foundTitle: What turned up along the way
gates.found1: On the Flow card the graph's simulation ends on different coordinates on arm64 and x64. It was green on the laptop and red in CI. Now the hash counts what the graph is made of, not where it lands.
gates.found2: The test config differed from production, so the gate stayed green while the server's 404 would have named itself and lost HSTS. The header block now matches line for line, and the gate looks at the 404's headers.
gates.found3: Gecko loses a thin diagonal gradient at random, and the hatching fell apart in Firefox. It is now an SVG mask, and a test keeps such gradients out of the stylesheets.
gates.found4: Shadows took the colour of the text, which on a dark page is a glow. In the dark mode a shadow is now transparent.
gates.found5: The story's test on home failed only in CI. It was a race in the scene itself: after a jump the ribbon was still catching up with the scroll, and the far photographs never woke. Now the reach is counted from where the scroll sends the ribbon.

decisions.name: Decisions
decisions.title: The decision first, the code next
decisions.p1: Whatever is expensive to undo is written down before the code: the context, the options, the choice and when to revisit it. An accepted record is never rewritten, a different decision is a new record.
decisions.p2: Static was not chosen to save money: the server had room. It is faster, more reliable and safer for the neighbour on that server, and the animation lives in the browser anyway. The repository has been open since the first commit, because what enters a history stays in old commits. The code is MIT, the texts and images are reserved, and GSAP stays a dependency that is never copied in.

process.name: Process
process.title: I decide, a tool writes
process.p1: A task begins in the plan and ends on the same branch: the checks, a PR, green CI and a fast-forward of <c>main</c>, every commit signed. A look is first chosen on a live HTML page of options in the real tokens, and only then does the site change. I look in Zen, on Gecko: some bugs live only there.
process.p2: Claude Code writes the code: it is a co-author of all {commits} commits in <c>main</c>. The repeated steps are skills in the repository, and the rules that may not be broken are in <c>CLAUDE.md</c>. What to build, how it looks and what goes live, I decide.
process.nt: start a task: a branch, the decisions, the build, the checks, a stop before the push
process.ar: audit whatever is not in main yet: bugs, motion, accessibility, budgets
process.si: land it: commits, a PR, CI, a fast-forward of main
process.rf: port a move from another site: describe it and write it anew in our tokens

release.name: Release
release.title: A release is one switch
release.p1: The site is a folder of files on a shared server, beside another product. A release touches neither Caddy nor the containers: a new build lands in a folder of its own, then one operation switches the <c>current</c> link. There is no downtime.
release.p2: The last three releases are kept, and <c>--rollback</c> returns the previous one in a second. GitHub holds no key to the server: CI only checks, and a release runs from the laptop. That is a price paid on purpose: there is one developer, and the site can be rebuilt from any commit.

stage.name: Stage
stage.title: What is not done yet
stage.p1: The site is a work in progress, and the plan in the repository shows it.
stage.item1: The Pora na Paru chapter on home still has stand-ins instead of screens.
stage.item2: The story's photographs are over budget: 2.12 MB in all against a limit of 1.5 MB, measured 01.11.2026.
stage.item3: The page change, the chapters on home and the Pora na Paru week have not been tested on a real iPhone or in real Safari.
